title: Authentication Fundamentals
summary: The factor model behind every login mechanism, and why MFA changes the security guarantee qualitatively rather than just adding a second hurdle. The foundation every later topic in this group builds on.

slides.markdown:
Every login mechanism — a password, a fingerprint, a hardware key — is an instance of the same underlying model: proving you are who you claim to be by presenting one or more **factors**. This topic covers that model, why combining factors is qualitatively stronger rather than just additively stronger, and a quick look at the modern alternatives to "just a password."

The distinction this topic opens with — **authentication vs authorization** — is the first thing interviewers check, in this group and beyond: authentication proves *who you are*; authorization decides *what you're allowed to do* once they know. Confusing the two is the single most common terminology slip in this space, and it's worth getting right from the start since every later topic in this group depends on the distinction staying clean.

slides.subTitle: The distinction interviewers always check first
slides.markdown:
**Authentication (AuthN)** answers "who are you" — logging in, proving your identity via a password, a biometric, a token. **Authorization (AuthZ)** answers "what are you allowed to do" — once your identity is established, does the system let you read this file, delete this record, access this admin panel.

The two are sequential and independent: you can be perfectly authenticated (the system genuinely knows you're user #4521) and still be authorized for almost nothing (a brand-new free-tier account). Conversely, a system with broken authorization but working authentication is exactly the [Broken Access Control](broken-access-control) failure from Application Security — the identity check passed, and the permission check is what failed.

HTTP status codes even encode this split: **401 Unauthorized** actually means "you're not authenticated" (despite the confusing name), while **403 Forbidden** means "you're authenticated, but not authorized for this." Getting that pairing right in an interview is a small, telling signal.

Every authentication mechanism reduces to proving control of one of three factor types:

- **Something you know** — a password, a PIN, the answer to a security question. Cheap to implement, but copyable: anyone who learns it can use it, and it can be phished, guessed, or leaked in a breach.
- **Something you have** — a phone that receives an SMS code, a hardware security key, an authenticator app generating rotating codes. Requires physical possession, which raises the bar past "knew a string" to "stole or cloned a device."
- **Something you are** — a fingerprint, face, or other biometric. Can't be "forgotten," but also can't be rotated if compromised — you can't issue yourself a new fingerprint the way you can reset a password.

A factor doesn't have to be perfect to be useful; each one just needs to raise a *different* kind of cost for an attacker to defeat. That's exactly why combining factor **types** (not two passwords) is the point of MFA, covered next.

slides.sectionTitle: Why MFA stops most credential-stuffing attacks
slides.markdown:
**Credential stuffing** is an attacker taking a breached username/password list from *one* site and trying those same pairs against *other* sites, betting on password reuse — and it works often enough to be one of the highest-volume attack types on the internet, entirely automatable at scale.

Multi-factor authentication (MFA) breaks this specific attack because it requires a **second, independent factor type** the attacker's breached list doesn't contain at all. Knowing the password is necessary but no longer sufficient — the attacker would also need the victim's phone, hardware key, or biometric, none of which leak in a typical password-database breach.

This is the qualitative shift mentioned in the snapshot: MFA isn't "20% harder to guess," it's "the attacker's entire stolen dataset, no matter how large, doesn't contain the second factor at all." That's why MFA adoption is the single highest-leverage authentication improvement most organizations can make, and why it's frequently mandated by compliance frameworks and cyber-insurance policies alike.

slides.sectionTitle: TOTP: a 6-digit code that rotates every 30 seconds
slides.markdown:
**TOTP** (Time-based One-Time Password) is how most authenticator apps (Google Authenticator, Authy, 1Password) generate their rotating codes, and the mechanism is elegantly simple: both the server and the app share a secret **seed** (exchanged once, usually via a QR code at setup), and both independently compute `HMAC(seed, current_time_step)` — truncated to a 6-digit code — using the current 30-second time window as input.

Because both sides compute the same function from the same seed and the same (roughly synchronized) clock, they arrive at the same code without ever transmitting it over the network during login. There's no round-trip to a server to "send" a code — the app just displays what it independently calculated.

This is also why TOTP fails if a device's clock drifts too far out of sync with the server's, and why losing the seed (a phone reset without exporting it first) means losing the ability to generate valid codes — which is precisely why setup flows show backup codes, a one-time fallback that doesn't depend on the seed at all.

Passwords are the weakest common factor — phishable, reusable, forgettable — which is why passwordless approaches are steadily displacing them for new products:

- **Magic links** — you enter your email, the service sends a one-time login link, clicking it authenticates you. This shifts "something you know" to "something you have access to" (your email inbox) without introducing a new device or app — simple, but only as secure as the email account backing it.
- **WebAuthn / passkeys** — a public-key credential is generated and stored on your device (phone, laptop, hardware key), unlocked locally by a biometric or PIN; only the **public** key is ever registered with the server. There's no shared secret transmitted at login at all, which structurally eliminates phishing: even a perfect fake login page can't extract a private key that never leaves your device, and can't reuse a signature captured from one site against another, since the signature is bound to that site's origin.

WebAuthn is the more significant shift of the two — it doesn't just relocate the "something you know" problem, it removes the shared-secret model that makes phishing possible in the first place.

The diagram makes the credential-stuffing defense visible directly: an attacker with a breached password can complete step 1 identically to the real user, but has no path through step 2 at all — that's the wall MFA adds, not a probabilistic speed bump.

slides.sectionTitle: SMS OTP vs authenticator app vs hardware key
slides.markdown:
| | SMS OTP | Authenticator app (TOTP) | Hardware key (WebAuthn) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Factor type** | Something you have (phone number) | Something you have (device with seed) | Something you have (physical key) |
| **Main weakness** | SIM swapping — attacker ports your number to their SIM | Seed can be phished if the user is tricked into typing the code into a fake site | None practical at scale — phishing-resistant by design |
| **Works offline** | No — needs cell signal | Yes | Yes |
| **Setup friction** | Lowest — just a phone number | Low — one QR scan | Higher — must purchase and carry a physical device |

These are **not equally strong**, despite all being "a second factor": SIM swapping is a well-documented, real attack against SMS OTP specifically — attackers social-engineer a carrier into porting a victim's number, no access to the victim's actual phone required. TOTP is a meaningful step up since it doesn't depend on the phone network, but it's still a code a user can be tricked into typing into a phishing site. WebAuthn's phishing resistance comes from the browser cryptographically binding the credential to the origin — a fake site simply cannot obtain a usable signature, no matter how convincing it looks to the human.

slides.sectionTitle: "Has a password" is not "is securely authenticated"
slides.markdown:
The pitfall this whole topic sets up: treating password-based login as a solved, binary checkbox — either an app "has authentication" or it doesn't — rather than a spectrum of actual security guarantees.

An app with only a password, no rate limiting, and no MFA technically "has authentication" in the sense that a login form exists. But it offers essentially no resistance to credential stuffing, provides no defense if that one password is phished, and gives an attacker a single point of failure to defeat. "Has a password field" and "is securely authenticated" are very different claims, and interviewers probe exactly this gap — a candidate who says "we use passwords for auth" without mentioning rate limiting, hashing, or MFA is describing a login form, not a security posture.

The rest of this group fills in what a real posture requires: [Sessions & Cookies](sessions-cookies) for what happens after login succeeds, [Password Storage & Credential Security](password-storage) for what "a password" needs to mean server-side, and the token- and delegation-based models beyond that.

The factor model and the AuthN/AuthZ distinction from this topic underpin everything else in this group: [Sessions & Cookies](sessions-cookies) is about *maintaining* an authenticated identity across requests once the factors have been checked once. [Password Storage](password-storage) is about protecting the "something you know" factor server-side. JWT, OAuth2, and OpenID Connect are all different mechanics for carrying and delegating proof of that identity across services.

Keep the AuthN vs AuthZ split sharp as you move forward — nearly every later topic in this group sits cleanly on one side of that line or the other.
